results.result: PDAC is a deadly cancer with poor prognosis, often diagnosed late, resistant to therapies, and frequently associated with cachexia that contributes to patient frailty and poor outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 and C18-C24 establish the clinical context of PDAC through cited literature. These are well-established facts about PDAC epidemiology, prognosis, and cachexia prevalence supported by appropriate citations.

results.result: Cancer sarcopenia involves protein metabolism alterations, systemic inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction, though mitochondrial involvement in PDAC-induced muscle wasting had not been previously addressed.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C31 provide background on sarcopenia mechanisms with appropriate citations (C25-C29, C31) and identify the knowledge gap (C30) that motivates this study. The literature review is well-supported.

results.result: KIC mice spontaneously develop PDAC and cachexia by 9-11 weeks, showing weight loss, increased pancreas weight due to tumor, splenomegaly, and decreased weights of muscle, liver, and adipose tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C38 describe the KIC model phenotype with data from Figure 1B-D showing statistically significant changes (p<0.01 to p<0.0001, n≥15-17 mice). The model characterization is well-documented with appropriate statistics.

results.result: KIC mice exhibit muscle fiber atrophy with decreased cross-sectional area and fiber diameter without changes in fiber number, accompanied by accumulation of MuRF1 E3 ubiquitin ligase indicating increased proteolysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 and C89 demonstrate sarcopenia through histological analysis (Figure 2A-D) with statistical significance (p<0.01 to p<0.0001, n=5-8 mice). Both immunofluorescence and western blot confirm MuRF1 accumulation, providing converging evidence.

results.result: KIC mice show reduced muscle volume (21%) and absolute tetanic force (16%), but specific tetanic force is unchanged, indicating that force reduction is fully accounted by muscle loss without alteration in muscle quality.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C49 present MR-based functional measurements (Figure 3A) with appropriate statistics (n=5-7 mice, p<0.05 to p<0.001). The interpretation that muscle quality is preserved is logically derived from the proportional relationship between volume and force loss.

results.result: Twitch half-relaxation time is prolonged in tumor-bearing KIC mice, suggesting disturbed muscle biomechanical properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 report increased relaxation time (Figure 3B) with statistical significance. The interpretation of disturbed biomechanical properties is reasonable given the data, though the mechanism is not explored.

results.result: KIC mice show impaired mitochondrial oxidative function in vivo, evidenced by 43% longer PCr resynthesis time constant and 31% lower maximal oxidative capacity, with compensatory increase in glycolytic flux indicated by lower pH during exercise.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 present 31P-MR spectroscopy data (Figure 3C-D) with appropriate statistics and cited methodology (Kemp et al., 2015; Prompers et al., 2014). The interpretation linking τPCr to mitochondrial function and pH to glycolysis is well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: Isolated mitochondria from KIC muscles show decreased basal respiration, proton leak, and maximal respiration without noticeable differences in ATP production or spare respiratory capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 present Seahorse oxygraphy data (Figure 4A-C) with statistical analysis (p<0.05 to p<0.0001, n=10-11 mice). The selective impairment of certain respiratory parameters is clearly documented.

results.result: Mitochondrial respiratory complexes I, II, and IV show decreased activities and protein levels in KIC muscles, confirmed by enzymatic assays, western blotting, and immunofluorescence.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 demonstrate OXPHOS defects through multiple complementary methods (Figure 4D-F) with statistical significance (p<0.001 to p<0.0001, n=5-11 mice). The convergence of three independent techniques strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: KIC mitochondria are elongated with disorganized cristae, characterized by higher area and diameter and lower circularity, suggesting hyperfusion and defects in mitochondrial dynamics and quality control.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 present TEM analysis (Figure 5A-B) with quantitative morphometric data (p<0.0001, n=3 mice, 100 mitochondria/mouse). The interpretation of hyperfusion is reasonable based on the morphological changes, though direct functional assessment of dynamics is not provided.

results.result: Despite unchanged mitochondrial number per surface area, KIC muscles show a 49% decrease in mitochondrial mass and 66-72% decrease in mtDNA, suggesting defective mitochondrial genome homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 and C70-C73 present quantitative data on mitochondrial content (Figure 5C-E) with strong statistical significance (p<0.01 to p<0.0001, n=6-8 mice). The disproportionate loss of mtDNA relative to protein mass supports the interpretation of genome homeostasis defects.

results.result: KIC muscles show increased Mitofusins and OPA1 (fusion proteins) potentially related to elongated mitochondrial phenotype, and decreased PGC1α and TFAM involved in mitochondrial biogenesis and mtDNA maintenance.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 present western blot data (Figure 5F) for key mitochondrial homeostasis proteins. The link between increased fusion proteins and elongated morphology is plausible, though the sample size appears limited (n=4-5 mice) and quantification is not shown for all proteins.

results.result: Transcriptomic analysis reveals 2304 dysregulated genes including 177 mitochondrial genes, with upregulation of atrophy markers (MuRF1, MAFBx), downregulation of TCA cycle genes, dysregulation of lipid metabolism pathways, and upregulation of ROS defense genes including Nrf2.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C84 present RNA-seq results (Figure 6, supplements) with FDR<0.05 (n=4 mice/group). The analysis includes appropriate pathway enrichment and the findings are consistent with the phenotype. The interpretation of Nrf2 upregulation as oxidative stress marker is well-established.

results.result: Proteomic analysis reveals 154 dysregulated proteins with all ROS defense proteins downregulated at the protein level despite upregulated genes, suggesting an altered response to oxidative stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 present proteomic data (Figure 7, supplements) with p<0.05 (n=4-5 mice/group). The discordance between transcript and protein levels for ROS defense is interesting but the interpretation (C87) is speculative ('could suggest'). Additional validation or mechanistic investigation would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Dlst (TCA cycle enzyme) is the only gene/protein found downregulated in both transcriptomic and proteomic analyses.
results.evaluation: Claim C88 identifies a specific gene/protein with concordant regulation across omics platforms. This is a straightforward observation from the data comparison (Table 1).

results.result: The study findings are consistent with prior literature on cancer cachexia, including mitochondrial morphology disruption and mtDNA decrease in cachectic patients, and suggest potential therapeutic approaches targeting lipid metabolism and physical activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C97 provide discussion context with appropriate citations. The comparison to human cachexia (C91-C92) and suggestions for therapeutic approaches (C93-C94, C97) are appropriately framed as speculative or requiring further investigation.

results.result: Cachectic PDAC KIC mice exhibit severe sarcopenia with mitochondrial dysfunction characterized by reduced respiratory capacities, structural alterations, and dysregulation of OXPHOS and mitochondrial dynamics, along with affected lipid and nucleic acid metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C13 summarize the main findings stated in the abstract. These are supported by the detailed experimental results presented in the manuscript (Figures 2-7) with appropriate statistical analysis and multiple complementary techniques.

results.result: KIC mice develop cachexia characterized by body weight loss, increased pancreas weight due to tumor replacement, splenomegaly, and decreased weights of gastrocnemius muscle, liver, and gonadal adipose tissue.
results.evaluation: Reviewers across all three reviews affirm the model's validity and cachexia phenotype. The editor states the study 'uses a mouse model of pancreatic cancer' and Reviewer 1 notes 'the authors utilize a genetically engineered mouse model of pancreatic cancer which recapitulates key aspects of human PDAC including the development of cachexia.' No concerns were raised about these basic characterization findings.

results.result: Histological analysis shows decreased muscle cross-sectional area and fiber diameter in KIC mice without changes in total fiber number, with moderate changes in fiber type proportions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 acknowledges 'muscle mass loss is associated with a diminution in muscle fiber's size, which is a common feature in cancer muscle wasting studies' and notes agreement that 'not all studies have demonstrated type 1 and 2 fiber differences.' The findings are accepted as consistent with the literature.

results.result: MuRF1 E3 ubiquitin ligase accumulates in KIC muscle as shown by immunohistofluorescence and western blotting.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 raises significant concern about the MuRF1 IHC staining, noting 'the MuRF1 IHC staining appears localized to the extracellular space surrounding blood vessels and myofibers-which causes concern as to the specificity of the antibody staining. MuRF1...would be expected to be expressed in the cytosol of muscle fibers.' This questions the validity of the immunofluorescence data, though western blot data is not specifically challenged.

results.result: Muscle volume and absolute tetanic force are reduced in KIC mice, but specific tetanic force (normalized to volume) is unchanged, indicating muscle quality is preserved and force reduction is due to muscle loss.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 summarizes these findings accurately in their summary without raising concerns: 'they found that phosphocreatine resynthesis and maximal oxidative capacity were reduced...during the recovery phase.' The functional measurements and their interpretation are accepted by reviewers.

results.result: Twitch half-relaxation time is prolonged in tumor-bearing KIC mice, suggesting disturbed muscle biomechanical properties.
results.evaluation: This finding is presented in the context of accepted functional measurements. Reviewer 2's summary acknowledges the comprehensive functional characterization without challenging this specific observation.

results.result: Post-exercise PCr resynthesis time constant is 43% longer in KIC mice, indicating altered mitochondrial function in vivo with 31% lower maximal oxidative capacity.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'By MR they found that phosphocreatine resynthesis and maximal oxidative capacity were reduced in the gastrocnemius muscle of tumor-bearing mice during the recovery phase.' This is presented as a key finding without challenge.

results.result: Lower pH at end of exercise in KIC mice suggests accelerated glycolytic flux.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'pH was reduced in muscle during the stimulation time' as part of the MR findings. The interpretation regarding glycolytic flux is accepted within the context of metabolic compensation discussed by reviewers.

results.result: Mitochondrial respiration measurements show decreased basal respiration, proton leak, and maximal respiration in KIC muscles, without changes in ATP production or spare respiratory capacity.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'By oxygraphy, the authors showed a decrease in basal respiration, proton leak, and maximal respiration in tumor-bearing mice' and describes the data as 'convincing.' Reviewer 1 notes 'the data are convincing and were collected and analyzed using state-of-the-art techniques.'

results.result: Activities of mitochondrial complexes I, II, and IV are decreased in KIC muscles, with corresponding decreases in OXPHOS protein abundance shown by western blotting and immunohistofluorescence.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 confirms 'a decrease of complex I, II, and IV activity, a reduction of OXPHOS proteins' as part of the comprehensive mitochondrial characterization. The editor notes the 'solid transcriptomics and proteomics approaches' support these findings.

results.result: KIC mitochondria are elongated with disorganized cristae, characterized by higher mean area and diameter and lower circularity, suggesting hyperfusion and defects in mitochondrial dynamics and mitophagy.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'mitochondria were elongated with disorganized cristae' as a key finding. Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'several morphological alterations of mitochondrial shape.' The structural observations are accepted, though the interpretation of dynamics is discussed further in relation to protein measurements.

results.result: The number of mitochondria per cell/surface is unchanged in KIC muscles.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'the total quantity of mitochondria from skeletal muscles of mice with pancreatic cancer cachexia is similar to controls.' This finding is accepted as distinguishing changes in mitochondrial mass from mitochondrial number.

results.result: Mitochondrial protein and DNA levels show remarkable decreases (twofold and threefold respectively) that outweigh total muscle mass loss, suggesting defective mitochondrial genome homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 confirms 'a reduction of...mitochondrial mass, mtDNA' as key findings. Reviewer 1 notes 'disruption of mitochondrial morphology and decrease of mtDNA were also observed in the skeletal muscle of cachectic patients,' supporting translational relevance. The interpretation of defective homeostasis is accepted.

results.result: Western blot analysis shows increased Mitofusins and OPA1 (fusion proteins) potentially related to elongated phenotype, and decreased PGC1alpha and TFAM (biogenesis and mtDNA maintenance proteins).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises major methodological concerns: 'The methodological approach to determining mitochondrial fusion and fission machinery shown in Fig. 5F is wrong. The correct way is to normalize the OPA1, MFn1/2 on mitochondrial proteins such as VDAC/porin.' They argue the normalization method creates artifacts and request analysis of OPA1 isoforms and DRP1 protein. This challenges the validity of the fusion/fission protein conclusions.

results.result: RNA sequencing reveals 2304 dysregulated genes including highly overexpressed atrophy markers (MuRF1/Trim63 and MAFBx/Fbxo32) and 177 dysregulated mitochondrial interactome genes.
results.evaluation: The editor emphasizes 'Most relevant are the solid transcriptomics and proteomics approaches to map out related changes in gene expression networks.' Reviewer 1 states 'unbiased proteomics and transcriptomics analyses supporting most of their conclusions.' The transcriptomic data quality and scope are affirmed.

results.result: Metabolic pathway analysis shows downregulation of half the TCA cycle genes and dysregulation of four lipid metabolism pathways in KIC muscles.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'the major strength of the paper is the bioenergetics and mitochondrial characterization associated with the transcriptomic and proteomic analyses' and highlights 'some novel metabolic insights such as nucleotide metabolism.' The lipid metabolism findings are accepted as novel contributions.

results.result: ROS defense genes including Nfe2l2 (encoding Nrf2) are upregulated in KIC muscles, marking oxidative stress.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'mitochondrial dysfunction can lead to increased production of ROS/oxidative stress' as an expected consequence. The upregulation of ROS defense genes is consistent with this framework and not challenged.

results.result: Proteomics shows 154 dysregulated proteins with all ROS defense proteins downregulated at protein level (opposite to gene upregulation), suggesting altered response to oxidative stress.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises a fundamental concern about transcriptome-proteome comparisons: 'The comparison of proteomic and transcriptomic profiles to identify concordance or not is problematic when atrophy programs are induced. In fact, most of the transcriptional-dependent upregulation is to preserve/maintain/reestablish enzymes that are consumed during enhanced protein breakdown.' This challenges the interpretation of discordance between mRNA and protein levels.

results.result: Dlst (TCA cycle enzyme) is the only gene found downregulated in both transcriptomic and proteomic signatures.
results.evaluation: This specific finding is presented as part of the comprehensive omics analysis. While Reviewer 3 raises concerns about transcriptome-proteome comparisons generally, this concordant downregulation is not specifically challenged.

results.result: Nucleic acid metabolism is affected in sarcopenic muscle of PDAC mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically highlights this as a strength: 'the major strength of the paper is...some novel metabolic insights such as nucleotide metabolism.' This is recognized as a novel contribution beyond previously known metabolic alterations.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising significant concerns about MuRF1 IHC antibody specificity and localization pattern. Major disagreement on immunofluorescence validity.

Both evaluate 31P-MR spectroscopy data on PCr resynthesis and oxidative capacity (C52-C54). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with appropriate statistics and well-supported interpretation. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge these findings as key results without challenge. Full agreement on SUPPORTED status.

Both address pH reduction and glycolytic flux interpretation (C55-C56). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with literature-backed interpretation. Peer reviewers accept pH findings and metabolic compensation interpretation. Full agreement on SUPPORTED status.

Both evaluate Seahorse oxygraphy data (C57-C61). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with clear documentation of selective respiratory impairment. Peer reviewers describe data as 'convincing' and collected using 'state-of-the-art techniques.' Full agreement on SUPPORTED status.

Both address OXPHOS defects demonstrated by multiple methods (C62-C64). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with convergence of three independent techniques. Peer reviewers confirm findings and note 'solid transcriptomics and proteomics approaches' support conclusions. Full agreement on SUPPORTED status.

OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with quantitative morphometric data, noting hyperfusion interpretation is reasonable though dynamics not directly assessed. Peer reviewers accept structural observations of elongated mitochondria with disorganized cristae. Agreement on SUPPORTED status.

Both address mitochondrial quantity findings (C14, C70). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED that total mitochondrial number is preserved. Peer reviewers explicitly state 'total quantity of mitochondria...is similar to controls,' distinguishing mass from number. Full agreement on SUPPORTED status.

Both evaluate mtDNA and mitochondrial mass reduction (C15-C17, C71-C73). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with strong statistical significance and interpretation of genome homeostasis defects. Peer reviewers confirm findings and note translational relevance to human cachexia. Full agreement on SUPPORTED status.

Both address fusion/fission protein measurements (C74-C77). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED though notes limited sample size and incomplete quantification. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising major methodological concerns about normalization approach and requesting analysis of OPA1 isoforms and DRP1. Significant disagreement on methodological validity.

Both evaluate RNA-seq results and pathway enrichment (C78-C80). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with appropriate FDR and pathway analysis. Peer reviewers emphasize 'solid transcriptomics' approaches and 'unbiased' analyses supporting conclusions. Full agreement on SUPPORTED status.

Both address lipid and nucleotide metabolism findings (C81-C82, C12). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as part of comprehensive RNA-seq analysis. Peer reviewers highlight 'novel metabolic insights such as nucleotide metabolism' as major strength. Full agreement on SUPPORTED status.

Both evaluate Nrf2 upregulation and ROS defense gene expression (C83-C84). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with well-established interpretation. Peer reviewers accept this as expected consequence of mitochondrial dysfunction without challenge. Full agreement on SUPPORTED status.

Both address transcriptome-proteome discordance for ROS defense (C85-C87). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting interpretation is speculative and needs validation. Peer reviewers also rate UNCERTAIN, raising fundamental concerns about comparing transcriptomic and proteomic profiles during atrophy programs. Agreement on UNCERTAIN status with similar concerns about interpretation.

Both evaluate concordant gene/protein regulation (C88). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as straightforward observation from data comparison. Peer reviewers accept this specific concordant finding despite general concerns about transcriptome-proteome comparisons. Agreement on SUPPORTED status.

Both address nucleotide metabolism as novel finding (C13). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as part of abstract summary backed by experimental results. Peer reviewers specifically highlight this as major strength and novel contribution. Full agreement on SUPPORTED status.
